pages.name: Slide to the change
pages.task: A 50 m cable run is made 60 m long. Slide the end of the bar until the tag shows its percentage change.
pages.why: The change is 60 − 50 = 10 m, and the start is 50 m. 10 ÷ 50 × 100 = 20%, so the end sits at 120%, up 20%.

pages.why: The change is £30 − £50 = −£20, and the start is £50. −20 ÷ 50 × 100 = −40%, a 40% cut.

pages.task: A supplier puts a £160 price up to £200. What is the percentage change?
pages.why: The change is £200 − £160 = £40, and the start is £160. 40 ÷ 160 × 100 = 25%. Dividing by the £200 would compare the rise with where it ended.

pages.task: A load rises from 40 A to 50 A, up 25%. It then falls back to 40 A. What is that percentage change?
pages.why: The fall is 10 A, but now the start is 50 A. −10 ÷ 50 × 100 = −20%. The same 10 A is a bigger share of the smaller 40 A, which is why the rise was 25%.

pages.task: An £80 part is now £68, and 68 ÷ 80 = 0.85. What is the percentage change?
pages.why: 68 ÷ 80 = 0.85, so £68 is 85% of the start. Take off the 100% you started with, 85% − 100% = −15%. The fall is £12, and 12 ÷ 80 × 100 = 15% too.

pages.task: The humidity in the plant room then goes from 50% to 60%. What is the percentage change?
pages.why: It is up 10 percentage points again, but the start is now 50%. 10 ÷ 50 × 100 = 20%, so the same 10 points is a smaller rise than before.

pages.task: Put it together. A 64 A load falls to 48 A. What is the percentage change?
pages.why: The change is 48 − 64 = −16 A, and the start is 64 A. −16 ÷ 64 × 100 = −25%, a 25% fall. As a check, 48 ÷ 64 = 0.75, so 48 A is 75% of the start.
